description: Driven by innovation, Elysion Group is tackling the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser. We are building an intuitive platform to analyze lunar landing sites and comms. Join the crew if you love space, code, or design!
summary: The purpose of our project "Elysion Lander" is to enable everyone to compare possible landing sites for a future moon mission. It addresses the challenge by providing a clean and simple to use UI that makes it possible for everyone to access all of this data. This is particularly important, because people understanding the difficulties of choosing a proper landing site brings them closer to the actual planning of the mission and the unique challenges of a moon mission. Our Website can help people realize and understand the significance of these new moon exploration Projects
details:
Project Details

Elysion Lander is a web tool for choosing a Moon landing site. We built it for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

What it does

The Mission Browser has five pages, one for each question a lander mission has to answer:

1. Landing Positions: a 3D Moon with six candidate sites near the south pole. They are ranked by 0.5 x Sun% + 0.3 x Earth% + 0.2 x Both%.

2. Sun & Earth: when the Sun and Earth are above the horizon at a site.

3. Solar Power: how many watts per square meter a panel could make.

4. Radio Link: how long a signal takes from the site to Earth and back.

5. Compare To: two sites side by side with graph comparison.

Benefits and impact

Users can compare sites by sunlight, power and radio contact instead of guessing. We hope this makes it easier to plan and to learn about lunar missions. All the data is real.

Tools

Front end: CesiumJS 1.146 for the 3D Moon, plus JavaScript, HTML and CSS.

Back end: Node.js, Express 5 and TypeScript.

Data: NASA JPL Horizons for positions. NASA LROC, LOLA and Moon Trek for the Moon surface, and NASA Deep Star Maps for the sky.

Documentation: written in Markdown and shown with marked.

What is creative

The Radio Link page doesn't use the simple "distance / speed of light x 2" estimate. Christian derived a first-order correction for asymmetric two-way light time. The Moon moves and the Earth rotates while the signal travels, so the way up and the way down differ. His code solves this with the Newton-Raphson method, using the Deep Space Network stations in Goldstone, Madrid and Canberra. A small letter icon travels along the Earth-Moon line at the calculated speed.

What we considered

Speed: Height data is decoded in Web Workers, long time ranges load in pieces, and results are cached.

Accuracy: Mountain shadows are not included yet, which was all documented properly.

Teamwork: Four people worked in parallel, so we split the code into separate files.

Honesty: We credit all sources and state where AI helped.
